title: Exploring nutrition misinformation on social media platforms
screen_reason: Conference abstract of a content analysis of 500 nutrition posts (250 Instagram, 250 TikTok) collected by keyword between 15 September 2023 and 15 March 2024 and coded for accuracy. One quantitative share with a recoverable denominator is reported: 'TikTok had a larger proportion of completely inaccurate posts (10.8%)' out of the 250 TikTok posts - a CONTENT estimate. The corresponding Instagram figure is described only qualitatively and cannot be extracted.

estimates.date: Collected over a six-month period from September 15, 2023, to March 15, 2024
estimates.measure_type: % of keyword-sampled TikTok nutrition posts coded as completely inaccurate
estimates.value_raw: TikTok had a larger proportion of completely inaccurate posts (10.8%)
estimates.denominator: 250 TikTok posts (half of the 500 posts analysed), retrieved with keywords such as healthy eating, healthy food, diet and weight loss over the six-month window
estimates.definition: Post assigned the 'completely inaccurate' level of the accuracy coding (as opposed to completely accurate or mostly accurate) under a modified Social Media Evaluation Checklist and an evidence coding framework
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition given; the abstract frames the object as 'unverified nutrition information' and 'nutrition misinformation', operationalised through an accuracy coding with a 'completely inaccurate' category
estimates.source_quote: TikTok had a larger proportion of completely inaccurate posts (10.8%), mainly related to weight loss.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (no page/section structure available - abstract-only text)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: "Posts were evaluated using a modified, previously developed, Social Media Evaluation Checklist (2) and evidence coding framework to measure accuracy." The abstract does not name the checklist's source, the number of coders, the training, or any inter-rater reliability statistic.
estimates.moderator_quote: A mixed-methods approach was employed, analysing 500 posts (250 from each platform) collected over a six-month period from September 15, 2023, to March 15, 2024, using keywords like healthy eating, healthy food, diet, and weight loss.
estimates.notes: The 250 denominator is inferred from '500 posts (250 from each platform)' - both figures verbatim, same denominator, so R8 is satisfied and no arithmetic beyond identifying which half applies. borderline = true because the instrument cannot be inspected: a 'Social Media Evaluation Checklist' is the kind of tool that mixes quality items (credentials, references, completeness) with accuracy items, and only the abstract is available. I coded CONTENT rather than QUALITY because the reported category is 'completely inaccurate', a falsity label that a wholly true post could not receive; if the full paper shows the accuracy levels are checklist-score bands rather than evidence-concordance judgements, this should be re-coded QUALITY. Note also that this is the STRICT end of a graded scale - the intermediate 'mostly accurate' band is not a clean true or false category, so 10.8% is a lower bound on inaccurate content by any broader definition.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The Instagram proportion of completely inaccurate posts is never given numerically ('Results indicated a higher prevalence of misinformation on TikTok compared to Instagram'), so the Instagram row that would naturally pair with the TikTok row cannot be extracted; likewise no pooled 500-post figure is stated. (2) The shares in the intermediate accuracy bands (completely accurate, mostly accurate) are not reported for either platform, so the full accuracy distribution is unavailable and 10.8% cannot be checked against a complement. (3) 'a significant portion (p < 0.05) of users lacking relevant credentials' gives no percentage and describes posters' credentials, not content falsity, so no row. (4) Engagement means (Instagram completely accurate 4,318 likes / 40 comments, mostly accurate 25,153 / 186; TikTok completely accurate 146,327 / 423, mostly accurate 75,804 / 483) are counts, not shares. (5) 'The most common characteristic was cooking/recipes and meal plans' is thematic, with no share. (6) ABSTRACT-ONLY CAVEAT for the adjudicator: how the 250 posts per platform were selected from the keyword results (top-ranked, most engaged, random?) is not described, so denom_selection was left blank; if the full text reveals a top-N or most-viewed selection, denom_selection should become 'curated'. The country/setting of the study is likewise unstated, hence country_norm = Global. Year is coded 2023 because collection began 15 September 2023, though the window straddles 2023-2024 (midpoint December 2023).

rob.design: Mixed-methods cross-sectional content analysis of 500 social media posts, 250 each from Instagram and TikTok, collected over six months (15 September 2023 - 15 March 2024) using keywords such as healthy eating, healthy food, diet and weight loss. Posts coded with a modified, previously developed Social Media Evaluation Checklist plus an evidence coding framework to measure accuracy, alongside poster credentials and engagement metrics; independent t-tests compared engagement across platforms and accuracy levels. Abstract-only: no information on how posts were selected within the keyword results, how many coders were used, coder training, inter-rater reliability, the accuracy rubric's thresholds, the country or language of the sample, or whether posts were deduplicated. Risk of bias cannot be properly appraised from this text.
